<reason>In a high-level debate, Side A wins by stays one step ahead on the underlying economic mechanisms and sequencing. Side B made a strong case that sixty years of raw-export dependence only built mine-to-port enclaves and that Africa already spends billions importing basic manufactures that regional industry could supply. However, Side A effectively neutralized both points in the second half: it showed that weak governance and high infrastructure costs ruin protected domestic manufacturing just as easily as resource rents (as seen in Nigeria's state refineries), that building regional factories still requires hard-currency imports of machinery and finance funded by global commodity exports, and that successful industrializers like Morocco and East Asia scaled by selling manufactures to rich global markets rather than relying primarily on low-income regional neighbors with covariant shocks.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's turnaround of the Nigerian refining and governance clash ([A2.1], [A4.1], [A4.6]): when Side B argued that Nigeria's fuel imports and failed refineries proved the failure of raw-export dependence, Side A showed that Nigeria owned refineries for decades that failed due to high operating costs and poor governance—and that if weak governance wastes resource rents, it will waste protected factory subsidies too ("Changing the customer does not fix governance").</best_rebuttal>
